about.title: Lakewood Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Lakewood is a city built around everyday errands. More than 81,000 people live here, and the shopping strips along Del Amo Boulevard, South Street, Woodruff Avenue, and Carson Street stay busy from morning through the evening rush. Every one of those grocery stores, restaurants, apartment complexes, and parking lots has an owner or manager responsible for keeping the place reasonably safe. When a spill sits unmarked, a walkway stays cracked, or a stairwell light goes dark, and someone gets hurt, California premises liability law applies. The key question is usually notice: did the owner know about the hazard, or should they have known, and did they fail to fix it or warn people? Proving that takes evidence, and evidence disappears fast. Surveillance video gets overwritten. Wet floors get mopped. Witnesses head home. LawProactive exists to shorten the gap between your fall and a conversation with an attorney who knows how to preserve what matters. We are not a law firm. We are a free service that connects Lakewood residents with an independent lawyer who works on contingency, so you owe nothing unless there is a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Lakewood Residents Turn to LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice Is the Heart of the Case
items.desc: California requires you to show the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard. The attorneys in our network know how to request inspection logs, maintenance records, and prior complaints that establish that knowledge.

items.title: Deadlines Are Shorter Than People Expect
items.desc: You generally have two years to file a premises liability claim in California, but if you fell on property owned by a public entity, the window to submit a claim is much shorter. Getting connected early protects your options.

items.title: Comparative Fault Does Not End Your Claim
items.desc: Under California's pure comparative fault rule, being partly responsible reduces your recovery rather than erasing it. An attorney can push back when an owner tries to pin all the blame on you.

items.question: I fell in a shopping center parking lot off Del Amo Boulevard. Who is actually responsible?
items.answer: It depends on who controls the specific area where you fell. A retail tenant may be responsible for its own entrance, while the property management company handles the common parking lot and walkways. An attorney can pull the lease terms and maintenance agreements to identify the right party, which matters because you need to show that party had notice of the hazard.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall in Lakewood if I am able?
items.answer: Photograph the exact spot, including the hazard and anything around it, before it gets cleaned or repaired. Ask for an incident report and get names of any employees or witnesses. Then seek medical care and reach out promptly, because many businesses keep surveillance footage for only a matter of days before it is recorded over.

items.question: I tripped on a broken sidewalk near a Lakewood park. Is that treated differently than a fall in a store?
items.answer: Yes, and the difference is significant. If the sidewalk or park is owned by the city, county, or another public entity, California requires you to file a government claim within a much shorter period than the standard two-year deadline. Missing that window can close off your claim entirely, so getting connected with an attorney quickly is especially important in these cases.
